source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2024 preprint) Prioritizing replay when future goals are unknown
finding: Defines the map hypothesis formally. The map is the Geodesic Representation (GR): a stack of goal-specific Q functions, one per candidate goal, each learned in an MDP where that goal is terminal and the only reward.
numbers: G(s,a,g) is the expected discounted return for taking a in s, then following the shortest-path policy to g. A single-goal GR equals Q-learning exactly. Discount 0.95 in most simulations.
limits: Tabular only. Gain is computed by brute-force enumeration of all possible backups, not by a plausible brain process. Goals assumed terminal and mutually exclusive.
agent_relevance: Store reusable routes to several candidate goals, not one value function for the current goal.
quote: learns paths that would be appropriate when generalizing to other goals

source: Sagiv et al. (2024 preprint) section 2.2: the priority rule
finding: Replay priority is the expected improvement summed over a belief distribution over goals: pick the memory that maximises E over g~P(g) of [H_post(s,g) - H_pre(s,g)]. Per goal it factorizes into need times gain, as in Mattar and Daw.
numbers: Need(sk,g) = discounted expected number of visits to sk under the goal-g policy (the SR under that policy). Gain = sum over actions of (pi_post - pi_pre) times G_post. One backup updates every goal page of the GR at once.
limits: How P(g) is learned is left open; the paper assumes simple Rescorla-Wagner estimates.
agent_relevance: Rank what to rehearse or cache by (how often a step is needed across likely goals) x (how much it improves routes): a memory priority weighted by goal belief.

source: Sagiv et al. (2024 preprint) result 3.1: asymmetric T-maze
finding: In a T-maze with a reward at the end of each arm (one arm shorter), the Q-value replay agent replays a path from the nearest reward to the start and stops. The GR agent replays paths from both goals, in order of distance.
numbers: Prioritized replay, discount 0.95, terminal rewards, single known start state. Qualitative result; no statistics reported.
limits: Stylised case with a known start and terminal rewards.
agent_relevance: A planner that caches only the route to the current goal loses the second route. Keeping both costs one extra replay.

source: Sagiv et al. (2024 preprint) result 3.1: bottleneck states
finding: When every state is a candidate goal and start, GR replay concentrates on bottleneck states shared by many shortest routes. GR need is a discounted variant of betweenness centrality. Interior corridor states are replayed less than their centrality predicts; the ends of bottlenecks are favoured.
numbers: Two mazes: two rooms joined by a narrow corridor, and a four-room community-graph maze. Replay distribution from n=250 simulated replay sequences (n=200 in Methods for the convergence runs); asymptotic need computed after GR convergence.
limits: Prediction not yet tested in animals. Simulation only.
agent_relevance: Prioritise hub steps that many goal routes pass through. Hubs are the cheapest high-coverage memory items.

source: Sagiv et al. (2024 preprint) result 3.2: simulated Gillespie task
finding: A GR agent with a fast behavioural goal estimate and a slow goal-distribution estimate reproduces both Gillespie findings: replay favours the previous block goal arm, and replay of the current goal arm rises across the block. The Mattar Q-learning agent shows the opposite on both.
numbers: Eight-arm maze; ns=200 sessions of nt=200 trials per agent. Two Rescorla-Wagner rates: fast for behaviour, slow for the goal distribution that drives replay. Small per-step decay of the GR. Replay learning rate 0.7. Comparison is qualitative against replotted data.
limits: Match is qualitative; no fit statistics. Result depends on the assumed slow learning rate and on GR decay. The authors say the decay gives replay a maintenance role.
agent_relevance: Two timescales: a fast tracker of the current goal for action and a slow estimate of the goal distribution for memory upkeep.

source: Sagiv et al. (2024 preprint) result 3.2: simulated Carey task
finding: GR replay reproduces Carey et al.: choice follows the deprived outcome but replay favours the other arm, because replay follows a slow across-session estimate. A Q-learning agent matches replay to behaviour.
numbers: na=10 virtual subjects, ns=6 sessions of alternating food/water restriction, nt=200 trials each. Asymmetric reward values swapped between sessions; replay learning rate 0.1.
limits: Qualitative match to a replotted figure. Small simulated N.
agent_relevance: Behaviour and memory upkeep can run on different value estimates and still be rational.

source: Sagiv et al. (2024 preprint) result 3.3: goal-switching prediction
finding: New prediction: the order of replay for current versus other goals depends on goal-switching statistics. After a blocked bottleneck with goal 1 active, GR replays g1 then g2 when p11 = 0.5, but g2 first when p11 = 0.05. Q-value replay only ever replans for g1.
numbers: Two-goal maze; the active goal each trial follows a Markov process with p11 = P(goal 1 stays active). Q-learning versus GR, both with prioritized replay. Simulation only.
limits: Untested in animals. The authors list it as a key future experiment.
agent_relevance: Plan for the goal likely to come back soon, not only the current one. Order of repair should follow the expected return of each goal.

source: Sagiv et al. (2024 preprint) discussion: predictions and limits
finding: Predictions: replay before any reward in latent learning; replay biased to central, topologically important states; goal replay scaled by goal statistics. Limits: tabular, gain by enumeration, goals terminal. A Default Representation (Piray and Daw) could serve as the target map instead.
numbers: No new animal data. The Zhou et al. temporal-context-model replay account is said to make similar predictions, since TCM associations coincide with the SR, which is the need term.
limits: Theory paper. Predictions are untested in the preprint.
agent_relevance: Value planning is the one-goal special case of map building. Our agent can treat current-goal-only as a special case of a weighted goal set.
quote: value replay arises as a special case of map replay when the agent's behavioural goals are fixed and known

source: Sagiv et al. (2024 preprint) section 2.1: why a route map instead of a local transition map
finding: The usual RL cognitive map is the one-step transition function, but replayed trajectories already reflect local connectivity even after new barriers, so replay cannot just be building that. A map of long-run routes to many goals gives replay a real job.
numbers: Argument only; no new numbers.
limits: Argument by definition of map; the claim depends on how map is defined.
agent_relevance: Store route-level results (shortest paths per goal) in addition to the edge list.

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Between planning and map-building: prioritizing replay when future goals are uncertain. Neuron
finding: Peer-reviewed version (issue date 17 Dec 2025, PMC12633763). Same GR theory and same two datasets. The summary now says whether replay prefers current goals (planning) or others (map) depends on their estimated likelihood of future relevance.
numbers: Based on the bioRxiv update posted 27 June 2025. Authors at Princeton, Oxford and UCL.
limits: Still tabular: reconciling with function approximation is called open. Simulations only; no new recordings.
agent_relevance: Citable source for the theory.
quote: Whether replay prefers current goals, like planning, or others, like maps, then depends on their estimated likelihood of future relevance.

source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay. Nat Neurosci
finding: The value-replay baseline that Sagiv extends. Replay order maximises Expected Value of Backup (EVB) = gain x need. Gain is the extra return from a policy change at the state. Need is the discounted expected future occupancy of the state, an SR quantity.
numbers: Dyna-style Q-learning in a linear track and Sutton's Dyna maze; learning rate 1.0, discount 0.9. Reproduces forward replay before a run, reverse replay after reward, more reverse replay for larger reward and fewer for zero reward, and decay of replay with experience.
limits: Single static reward function with goal-specific Q values. Goal-switching data of Gillespie and Carey challenge it (Sagiv 2025).
agent_relevance: Basis for a memory priority score: need x gain.
quote: the utility of a backup ... increase in reward following the target state multiplied by the expected number of times the target state will be visited

source: Gillespie, Astudillo Maya, Denovellis, Liu, Kastner, Coulter, Roumis, Eden, Frank (2021) Hippocampal replay reflects specific past experiences rather than a plan for subsequent choice. Neuron
finding: In a dynamic-goal eight-arm task, CA1 replay content did not predict the upcoming choice. It was enriched for the previous goal arm and depleted for recently visited arms.
numbers: N=4 Long-Evans rats; 24, 32, 23, 33 sessions. Goal arm moved after 4-15 rewards. Remote replay was 35.1%, 41.1%, 34.5%, 47.2% of SWR events per rat. Previous-goal arm made up about 20% of pre-choice remote replay in search trials. About 95% of SWRs had spatially continuous content. Poisson GLMs with 99% CIs; 711-1065 search trials and 1154-1730 repeat trials per rat.
limits: Four rats, one lab. The authors admit task details may contribute. Local replay near the current position is also common (about 80% of events start near the animal).
agent_relevance: A memory biased toward the last goal is not necessarily broken: it may be route upkeep.
quote: Replay is poorly suited to guiding immediately subsequent behavior

source: Gillespie et al. (2021): correct versus error trials and agreement with other studies
finding: A cross-validated binomial GLM could not reliably separate correct from error trials using counts of future-arm or current-goal replay. Authors cite Carey 2019, Gupta 2010 and Olafsdottir 2015 as consistent with replay of non-preferred and not-recently-visited locations.
numbers: Trials subsampled to 50% chance; 848, 1308, 614, 780 trials per subset per rat; 1000 subsamples; Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.
limits: A null for planning, which is hard to prove with four animals.
agent_relevance: Do not accept a stated plan as the cause of the choice; check the output.

source: Carey, Tanaka, van der Meer (2019) Reward revaluation biases hippocampal replay content away from the preferred outcome. Nat Neurosci (bioRxiv 2018 text read)
finding: On a T-maze with food on the left and water on the right, rats chose the outcome they were deprived of, but hippocampal SWR content was biased toward the other arm.
numbers: N=4 male rats; 193 food and 197 water choices overall. Food-restricted days 89% food choices, water-restricted days 80% water choices (chi2 df=3 = 188.7, p<.05). Significant events only: food-restriction sessions 0.28 food vs 0.72 water; water-restriction sessions 0.53 food vs 0.47 water; interaction F=8.53, p=.006. Mixed model likelihood-ratio test for motivational state 10.1, p=.0015.
limits: Small N; 15-20 trials per session. Sequenceless decoding gives the main result. Water-restriction bias is weak (0.53 vs 0.47).
agent_relevance: Counterexample to memory follows current goal. Supports keeping the non-preferred route warm.
quote: SWR content was systematically biased in the direction opposite rats' behavioral preferences

source: Carey et al. (2019): motivational state and pre-task bias
finding: Adding motivational state improved a second model of SWR content (likelihood-ratio 4.27, p=.038). One analysis found content bias already in pre-task rest, before experience that day (chi2 df=3 = 30.1, p<.001), so content is set partly by earlier experience.
numbers: Figures as printed in the 2018 preprint; some tests use the sequence-detection subset.
limits: Preprint figures may differ from the final Nat Neurosci version. No independent replication was found in the searches done.
agent_relevance: Memory content is partly set before the task by past experience.

source: Ambrose, Pfeiffer, Foster (2016) Reverse replay of hippocampal place cells is uniquely modulated by changing reward. Neuron
finding: Reverse replay rate rose with increased reward and fell with decreased reward at a track end; forward replay did not change. This is a main support for value-driven reverse replay used by Mattar and Daw.
numbers: Experiment One: reward 4x at one end in epoch 2. Experiment Two: reward 0 at one end. 15-20 laps per epoch, three epochs per day. Rates shown as means with 95% CIs.
limits: Free-running familiar track; it does not test whether replay content follows the current goal. Animal numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Reward size changes consolidation strength, not which route is kept.
quote: only reverse replays increased their rate at increased reward, or decreased their rate at decreased reward, while forward replays were unchanged

source: Russek, Momennejad, Botvinick, Gershman, Daw (2017) Predictive representations can link model-based RL to model-free mechanisms. PLoS Comput Biol
finding: Introduces Dyna-SR: the successor representation updated by replayed transitions. SR plus TD handles reward revaluation but not transition (detour) change; replay-based updates repair part of this.
numbers: Simulated Tolman-style tasks: latent learning, reward devaluation, sensory preconditioning (reward change); detour and contingency degradation (transition change). Preventing replay slows acquisition for both SR-Dyna and Dyna-Q.
limits: Simulation. The SR depends on the policy, so it is not a clean goal-general map; the GR addresses this.
agent_relevance: Pre-computed predictions cut decision time but go stale when structure changes; replay is needed to refresh them.

source: Momennejad, Russek, Cheong, Botvinick, Daw, Gershman (2017) The successor representation in human reinforcement learning. Nat Hum Behav
finding: Humans revalued more after a reward change than after a transition change, as an SR predicts, though both beat control.
numbers: N=58 participants. Revaluation scores: reward 0.5199 (SEM 0.0203), transition 0.4503 (SEM 0.0229), control 0.0310 (SEM 0.0310). Reward vs transition t(57)=2.89, p<0.01; reward vs control t(57)=10.14; transition vs control t(57)=9.05; control vs zero t(57)=1.2, p=0.22.
limits: The gap is modest (0.52 vs 0.45). Behaviour only; no replay measured.
agent_relevance: Cached predictions give goal-flexible but structure-rigid behaviour, a known failure for a cached-route agent.

source: Piray and Daw (2021) Linear reinforcement learning in planning, grid fields, and cognitive control. Nat Commun
finding: Default Representation: a temporally abstracted map of future occupancy under a default policy, reused across goals. The value of any state under any goal is a weighted average of default-policy occupancies. Sagiv names it as an alternative target for map replay.
numbers: Linear RL replaces nonlinear optimisation with a linear approximation softly biased toward the default policy. Learnable by experience or replay with a TD rule. Simulations; no single N.
limits: Model paper; the cost is a bias toward the default policy.
agent_relevance: Cheap closed-form re-planning for a new goal without new search.
quote: It replaces the classic nonlinear, model-based optimization with a linear approximation

source: Mallory, Widloski, Foster (2026 preprint) Spatial goals trap hippocampal replay. bioRxiv
finding: Rat data: replay occurred nearly twice as often during reward at the single consistently rewarded Goal as at Non-Goal sites, and replays slowed and ended near the Goal. They argue for an adaptation-based mechanism.
numbers: Abstract only (via bioRxiv and Europe PMC APIs). Sample sizes not read.
limits: Preprint, abstract only. Not a test of the GR theory.
agent_relevance: Reward-linked sites attract memory.

source: Widloski and Foster (2022) Flexible rerouting of hippocampal replay sequences around changing barriers in the absence of global place field remapping. Neuron
finding: When barriers and goals moved between sessions, replays depicted new goal-directed paths around barriers with no global place-cell remapping.
numbers: Abstract only (Europe PMC). No numbers read.
limits: Abstract only. Goal-directed content is something a map view must also explain.
agent_relevance: Replay content updates quickly to new structure; supports replay as map updating.

source: Pfeiffer and Foster (2013) Hippocampal place-cell sequences depict future paths to remembered goals. Nature
finding: Classic support for the planning view: sequences before movement depicted future paths to remembered goal locations.
numbers: Not opened this session; no numbers quoted.
limits: Not read. Later work (Gillespie 2021) found replay that does not predict the upcoming choice in a different task.
agent_relevance: Planning-like replay exists but is not the only content.

source: Dayan (1993) Improving generalization for temporal difference learning: the successor representation. Neural Computation
finding: Origin of the successor representation, a pre-computed expected discounted future occupancy that generalises across reward functions.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Known only through citations in the papers I read.
agent_relevance: The idea behind the need term.

source: Reading across the three rat datasets (Ambrose 2016, Gillespie 2021, Carey 2019)
finding: Ambrose reward-size effects fit value replay. Gillespie and Carey (replay lags or opposes behaviour) challenge a tight link between replay and current choice. Sagiv argues both fit one theory with two timescales.
numbers: Ambrose: free-running track. Gillespie: N=4, dynamic goal. Carey: N=4, deprivation switch. All are small-N rat studies from three labs.
limits: My synthesis, not a claim of one paper. No independent replication of the lag or bias was found in my searches.
agent_relevance: Compatible with a slow-goal-prior memory. Mark as [S] in the schema.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in Large Language Models with CogEval, arXiv 2309.15129
finding: Eight LLMs on map and planning tasks built from human experiments. They list local edges well but hallucinate edges, take longer routes and loop on community graphs. The authors say this does not support emergent planning.
numbers: Models: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, davinci-003, Bard, Cohere-52.4B, Claude-1-52B, LLaMA-13B, Alpaca-7B. Shortest path to a state one cluster away: GPT-4 succeeded 0 of 30 runs at temperature 0, and at most 10% at temperature 0.5 or 1.
limits: 2023 models only. Graph tasks, not replay. BFS or chain-of-thought prompts helped only in part.
agent_relevance: LLMs know the local edges but do not unroll routes reliably, so build the goal-general route table in code, not in the model.
quote: These findings do not support the idea of emergent out-of-the-box planning ability in LLMs

source: Hu, Van Durme, Andreas, Jhamtani (2025) Sample-Efficient Online Learning in LM Agents via Hindsight Trajectory Rewriting (ECHO), arXiv 2510.10304
finding: ECHO adapts hindsight experience replay for LM agents: after a failed episode the model proposes alternative goals the trajectory could have reached and rewrites optimised trajectories for them, kept in compressed memory. This is route memory for goals other than the current one.
numbers: GPT-4o. On XMiniGrid-Stateful ECHO had the highest mean reward and beat Reflexion and AWM; up to 80% above the vanilla ReAct baseline across both domains. Imputed workflows reached their imputed goals 34 of 40 times (85%). On PeopleJoinQA Reflexion was slightly more accurate; ECHO and AWM used about 1.6 fewer messages.
limits: Two benchmarks, one model. No method dominated across PeopleJoin organisations. 6 of 40 imputed workflows failed (4 agent deviations, 2 infeasible steps). Not a test of the GR theory; HER is the engineering analogue.
agent_relevance: Closest working LLM analogue: keep routes to alternative goals, not only the current one. Gains were real but uneven.
quote: ECHO generates optimized trajectories for alternative goals that could have been achieved during failed attempts
